utterances.speaker: HOST
utterances.text: Welcome back to the show. I'm here with Dana, who I've been trying to get on for about a year now.

utterances.speaker: GUEST
utterances.text: Thanks for having me. Long overdue.

utterances.speaker: HOST
utterances.text: How was the flight in?

utterances.speaker: GUEST
utterances.text: Fine, delayed a bit, but fine. Slept most of it.

utterances.speaker: HOST
utterances.text: Good. So let's start at the beginning. Walk me through the early days.

utterances.speaker: GUEST
utterances.text: So we started in 2019, two of us, working out of my apartment in Oakland.

utterances.speaker: HOST
utterances.text: And what was the product at that point?

utterances.speaker: GUEST
utterances.text: Honestly it was a spreadsheet with a login screen bolted on top. That was it.

utterances.speaker: GUEST
utterances.text: We hit a hundred thousand dollars in revenue in the first eleven months, which nobody believed.

utterances.speaker: HOST
utterances.text: From a spreadsheet.

utterances.speaker: GUEST
utterances.text: From a spreadsheet. We scaled it to 2.4 million ARR before we wrote a single line of real backend code.

utterances.speaker: HOST
utterances.text: That's genuinely absurd.

utterances.speaker: GUEST
utterances.text: It is absurd. And it worked because we were solving something people were already doing manually.

utterances.speaker: GUEST
utterances.text: Then in 2021 we raised a Series A. Eighteen million dollars. That was the worst decision I have ever made.

utterances.speaker: HOST
utterances.text: Wait, the raise was the mistake?

utterances.speaker: GUEST
utterances.text: The raise was the mistake. We went from twelve people to ninety in seven months and we almost went bankrupt doing it.

utterances.speaker: GUEST
utterances.text: I lost everything I'd built. The culture, the speed, all of it. We burned fourteen million dollars in nineteen months and had almost nothing to show for it.

utterances.speaker: HOST
utterances.text: How close did you actually get?

utterances.speaker: GUEST
utterances.text: Eleven days of runway. I was terrified. I genuinely thought I was going to have to tell ninety people they were out of a job before Christmas.

utterances.speaker: GUEST
utterances.text: Here's what nobody tells you about venture funding. The money isn't the product. The money is a deadline.

utterances.speaker: GUEST
utterances.text: I've never said this publicly, but our board pushed us to hire a VP of Sales who cost us about eight months and two million dollars, and I knew it was wrong when I signed the offer.

utterances.speaker: HOST
utterances.text: Why did you sign it then?

utterances.speaker: GUEST
utterances.text: Because I was twenty-nine and I thought the adults in the room knew something I didn't. They did not.

utterances.speaker: GUEST
utterances.text: Unpopular opinion: most seed-stage startups should never raise institutional money at all.

utterances.speaker: HOST
utterances.text: That's going to annoy a lot of your investors.

utterances.speaker: GUEST
utterances.text: Probably. But it's true. Venture capital is a specific instrument for a specific shape of business and everyone treats it like it's oxygen.

utterances.speaker: HOST
utterances.text: I think that's completely wrong, actually.

utterances.speaker: GUEST
utterances.text: Go on.

utterances.speaker: HOST
utterances.text: No, that's not what the data says. The companies that get to real scale are overwhelmingly venture backed.

utterances.speaker: GUEST
utterances.text: You're missing the point. I'm not saying nobody should raise.

utterances.speaker: HOST
utterances.text: That is what you said. You said most startups shouldn't raise.

utterances.speaker: GUEST
utterances.text: Let me finish. I said most seed-stage startups. There's a difference and you're flattening it.

utterances.speaker: HOST
utterances.text: With all due respect, that's a distinction you invented thirty seconds ago.

utterances.speaker: GUEST
utterances.text: It's a distinction that cost me eighteen million dollars to learn, so I'd argue I've earned it.

utterances.speaker: HOST
utterances.text: Okay, fair enough. Let me steelman your position for a second.

utterances.speaker: GUEST
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: HOST
utterances.text: The counterargument to my point is that survivorship bias makes venture look better than it is. We only ever see the ones that worked.

utterances.speaker: GUEST
utterances.text: That's exactly it. On the other hand, I take your point that at a certain scale you genuinely cannot self-fund.

utterances.speaker: HOST
utterances.text: Right, so where I'd push back is on the timing, not the principle.

utterances.speaker: GUEST
utterances.text: Both things can be true. Raise late, raise less, raise from people who've operated.

utterances.speaker: GUEST
utterances.text: You know what the funniest part of the near-death experience was?

utterances.speaker: HOST
utterances.text: I can't imagine anything about that being funny.

utterances.speaker: GUEST
utterances.text: We had this all-hands where I was going to tell everyone how bad it was, and the projector broke.

utterances.speaker: GUEST
utterances.text: So I'm standing there with a slide deck about our imminent collapse and the IT guy is crawling under the table going, is it plugged in? [laughs]

utterances.speaker: HOST
utterances.text: [laughs] Oh, that's terrible.

utterances.speaker: GUEST
utterances.text: It was terrible. It was also the moment I stopped panicking, weirdly.

utterances.speaker: HOST
utterances.text: So what actually saved you?

utterances.speaker: GUEST
utterances.text: We cut sixty percent of the team in one day and went back to the spreadsheet.

utterances.speaker: GUEST
utterances.text: Not literally, but philosophically. We asked what the twelve of us would build, and we built that.

utterances.speaker: HOST
utterances.text: And that worked.

utterances.speaker: GUEST
utterances.text: We were profitable fourteen months later and we've never raised again.

utterances.speaker: GUEST
utterances.text: The lesson here is that headcount is not progress. I confused the two for about two years and it nearly killed the company.

utterances.speaker: GUEST
utterances.text: If I could go back, I'd tell myself to stay small for twice as long as feels comfortable.

utterances.speaker: HOST
utterances.text: That's good advice.

utterances.speaker: GUEST
utterances.text: My advice would be simpler than that, actually. Before you hire anyone, write down what specifically gets worse if you don't.

utterances.speaker: GUEST
utterances.text: If you can't answer that in one sentence, you don't need the hire. You need a decision you're avoiding.

utterances.speaker: HOST
utterances.text: Last question. Was it worth it?

utterances.speaker: GUEST
utterances.text: I'll never forget standing in the parking lot after the layoffs. That was the hardest day of my life, and I did it to myself.

utterances.speaker: GUEST
utterances.text: So, worth it? The company survived. But I don't think I get to call it worth it. I think I just get to not do it again.

utterances.speaker: HOST
utterances.text: Dana, thank you. This was great.

utterances.speaker: GUEST
utterances.text: Thanks for having me.
